These are my answers to the Chapter 9 checkpoint questions. The example pages show some of the form controls discussed in the chapter.

Checkpoint 1 - Basic Forms (page 20)

1. Should the store use two or three input boxes for a customer email list?

I would use three input boxes: first name, last name, and email. This keeps the names organized and makes it easier to sort customers later. It also lets the store address someone by their first name in an email.

2. What form control would work for a survey with ten choices and only one answer?

I would use a drop-down list with the select element. It lets the person choose one answer without taking up too much space on the page.

3. True or false: The value attribute makes radio buttons work as a group.

False. Radio buttons are grouped by using the same name attribute. The value attribute tells which answer was chosen.

See the customer sign-up example and the survey example.

Checkpoint 2 - Accessible Forms (page 29)

1. What do the fieldset and legend elements do?

A fieldset puts related form controls into a group. The legend gives that group a title, so it is easier to understand what the questions are about.

2. What is the purpose of accesskey, and how does it help accessibility?

The accesskey attribute gives a form control a keyboard shortcut. This can help people who use the keyboard instead of a mouse get to a field faster.

3. Would you use a submit input, image button, or button element? Does accessibility differ?

I would usually use a normal submit button because it is simple and easy to recognize. A button element can work just as well if it has clear text. An image button needs useful alt text so people using screen readers know what it does.

See the contact form example.

Checkpoint 3 - Server-Side Processing (page 41)

1. Describe server-side processing.

Server-side processing happens after a website sends information to a server. A program on the server can use the data, save it in a database, or send an email and then return a response.

2. Why do the server-side developer and web page designer need to communicate?

They need to make sure the form sends the right information to the right place. They should agree on things like the field names, required information, and what should happen after the form is submitted.
